title: Small but Mighty: Test Suites as Improvement Signalsfor Self-Evolving Agents

paper.title: Small but Mighty: Test Suites as Improvement Signals for Self-Evolving Agents
paper.abstract:
Abstract A self-evolving agent rewrites its own harness and must decide which rewrites to
keep, so its improvement signal is the check a rewrite has to pass. Verifying a rewrite by agent rollout is expensive and subjective, while
executable checks such as the repository’s own tests are too sparse to catch
behavior-changing rewrites, rejecting only a quarter of them. We instead take test feedback as the
executable signal, and search for test suites that are both small and strong
with a quality–diversity evolutionary algorithm, so that the signal is dense
and informative. tesearch treats suite size as a behavior descriptor, so that quality is
pursued at every size and a small, strong suite is reachable, and learns a
transition kernel during the search that denoises the LLM as an actuator on
that descriptor.
Across 129 129 real-world modules and three backbones, tesearch delivers the highest-quality suites of any method compared,
LLM-driven evolutionary search included, and the smallest of any LLM-based one.
Used as the improvement signal of a self-evolving agent, it rejects 59.9 % 59.9\% of
behavior-changing rewrites against 25.3 % 25.3\% for the repository’s tests, at a 4.0 % 4.0\% false-alarm rate and 3.5 3.5 s per decision. The code and data are
available at https://github.com/ccsnow127/TeSearch .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Self-evolving agents get stronger by editing the code that runs them: the harness that prompts the model, parses its actions, executes them and records the trajectory [ 34 , 55 , 67 ] . The check a rewrite must pass to be kept is the agent’s improvement signal . Accept a rewrite that silently changes behavior and every later episode and rewrite inherits it; reject rewrites that preserve behavior and the evolution stalls. In software engineering the executable form of this check is the test suite, a regression specification [ 62 ] that captures the accepted behavior of the code so that later modification can preserve it. The signals available today are weak. Accepting on rollout outcome spends an agent episode per candidate on a noisy end-to-end score. The repository’s own tests are free, but they were written before the agent existed and anticipate none of its edits: we find them rejecting only 25.3 % 25.3\% of the rewrites that change behavior ( Section 5.3 ). A generated suite can do better, but only if it is effective , so that a behavioral change breaks at least one test, and efficient , since it runs on every proposed rewrite and its failures are read by a model with a finite context. Existing generators, search-based or LLM-based, optimize effectiveness and leave size to whatever emerges [ 18 , 35 , 2 , 24 ] . We formulate size-optimized unit test generation and, rather than scalarizing quality against size, let size define where a suite competes and quality whether it wins : size is a behavior descriptor of a quality–diversity (QD) search [ 39 , 45 ] , so the small end stays alive instead of being eliminated by the large one. Two challenges follow. LLM calls are expensive, so a finite budget must be allocated across niches whose value is unknown. And unlike classical QD, the descriptor cannot be set directly: the search can only ask the LLM for a count, which LLMs follow imprecisely [ 71 ] , so the niche a call targets and the niche it lands in differ. tesearch answers both: an online landing kernel models the LLM as a noisy actuator on the descriptor, correcting its bias and predicting where each call lands, and a size-annealing UCB allocates calls across niches from those predictions, turning toward smaller suites only once quality is secured. Its suites are the strongest and, among LLM-based methods, the smallest on 129 129 real-world modules, and as the improvement signal of a self-evolving agent they more than double the detection of behavior-changing rewrites at a cost the loop can afford on every one.

sections.heading: 2 Related work
sections.text: Self-evolving agents and improvement signals. Self-improving LLM systems differ first in where an improvement is written. Weight-space methods fine-tune the model on its own data or rewards [ 56 , 74 , 73 ] , a gain that cannot be read, diffed or reverted. Context-space methods write into the harness instead, through verbal self-refinement [ 37 , 49 ] , prompt search and textual gradients [ 60 , 64 , 44 , 1 ] , experience memory [ 68 ] , skill synthesis [ 54 ] or search over the whole scaffold [ 22 ] ; at the frontier the agent rewrites its own code, including the procedure that performs the update [ 17 , 65 , 67 , 34 ] . What decides whether an improvement is kept ranges from the model’s own judgment [ 6 , 63 ] to external verifiers such as tests [ 7 , 9 ] , compilers [ 29 , 20 ] and environments [ 36 ] . Tests are the signal coding agents such as Cursor, Codex and Claude Code [ 4 , 42 , 3 ] lean on across whole repositories [ 26 , 61 , 66 ] , yet they are taken as given: the repository’s own or written ad hoc. We optimize the test signal itself, for the strength and cost a loop running it on every rewrite needs. See Appendix F for additional related work. Evolutionary and quality–diversity search. LLMs used as variation operators under executable fitness make evolutionary search a strong inference-time optimizer [ 47 , 41 , 28 ] , but a global objective concentrates the population around one mode [ 19 , 16 ] . QD optimization instead partitions the search space by behavior descriptors and optimizes quality within each region [ 30 , 15 ] : MAP-Elites keeps an elite per cell [ 39 ] , and MOME a Pareto front per cell whose hypervolumes it sums [ 45 ] . Search-based test generation evolves program inputs against coverage goals [ 18 , 35 ] and test-suite reduction shrinks a written suite post hoc [ 21 , 48 ] ; neither controls size during generation. In classical QD the descriptor is read off what an individual turns out to be; here it must be requested from an LLM before it can be observed, and tesearch models that actuation error explicitly.

sections.heading: 3 Size-optimized test generation
sections.text: Given a Python module M M , a suite T T is a finite set of test functions for M M , with size s ⁡ ( T ) s(T) . With the origin as reference, a suite has hypervolume hv ⁡ ( T ) = c ⁡ ( T ) ​ m ​ ( T ) \mathrm{hv}(T)=c(T)\,m(T) [ 72 ] , high only when both objectives are. Definition 1 is the terminal objective; QD is the search surrogate. Larger suites are naturally advantaged in a global competition on ( c , m ) (c,m) [ 40 , 23 ] , so size becomes the behavior descriptor and quality is optimized independently within size niches, each keeping a Pareto front over ( c , m ) (c,m) rather than a single elite [ 45 ] : 𝒜 j = nd ( c , m ) { T ∈ 𝒯 : b j − 1 ≤ s ( T ) < b j } , j = 1 , … , K , \mathcal{A}_{j}=\operatorname*{nd}_{(c,m)}\big\{\,T\in\mathcal{T}:b_{j-1}\leq s(T)<b_{j}\big\},\qquad j=1,\dots,K, (1) where nd \operatorname{nd} takes the non-dominated subset and b 0 < ⋯ < b K b_{0}<\dots<b_{K} are the niche boundaries, the outermost two left open ( b 0 = 0 b_{0}=0 , b K = ∞ b_{K}=\infty ). The niches are geometric, since the variation in generated size grows with the size requested ( Appendix A ). Search loop and challenges. Each iteration ( Figure 1 ) selects a target niche; takes as parents the Pareto-front suite nearest the target in log size on each side of it, ordered weaker to stronger since an LLM weighs its most recent context most; prompts the LLM with the parents, the module annotated with its uncovered lines and surviving mutants, and the target size ( Appendices C and D ); then scores the suite and files it where it actually lands ( Algorithm 1 ). The two challenges are allocation of the call budget and actuation .

sections.heading: 4 tesearch
sections.text: Figure 1: Overview of tesearch . The archive (bottom) keeps a Pareto front on (coverage, mutation score) per size niche. (1) Size-UCB picks a target niche through the transition kernel; (2) the nearest front suite on each side of the target size becomes a parent; (3) parents, module, execution feedback and target size form the context; (4) the LLM writes a suite, possibly off the requested size; (5) the suite is filed where it lands, and the size error updates the kernel.

sections.heading: The landing kernel.
sections.text: Requesting a suite of size a a may produce one of size s ≠ a s\neq a , so a call aimed at one niche may land in another and credit assigned to the target goes to the wrong arm. LLMs follow count instructions with multiplicative noise [ 69 , 31 , 58 ] , so we model landing in log space, ln ⁡ s ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( ln ⁡ a + δ , σ 2 ) , \ln s\;\sim\;\mathcal{N}\big(\ln a+\delta,\ \sigma^{2}\big), (2) with δ \delta the systematic count bias and σ \sigma the residual spread. The bias varies across modules and backbones and enters the request directly, so it is estimated online and compensated before generation: for a target niche k k with center τ k = b k − 1 ​ b k \tau_{k}=\sqrt{b_{k-1}b_{k}} , inverting Equation 2 gives the request ln ⁡ a k = ln ⁡ τ k − δ \ln a_{k}=\ln\tau_{k}-\delta , rounded to an integer. The spread only spreads credit over neighboring niches; it is stable and fixed at its holdout median. The landing distribution of a call aimed at niche k k is p j ​ ( k ) = Φ ⁡ ( ln ⁡ b j − μ k σ ) − Φ ⁡ ( ln ⁡ b j − 1 − μ k σ ) , μ k = ln ⁡ a k + δ , p_{j}(k)=\Phi\!\Big(\tfrac{\ln b_{j}-\mu_{k}}{\sigma}\Big)-\Phi\!\Big(\tfrac{\ln b_{j-1}-\mu_{k}}{\sigma}\Big),\qquad\mu_{k}=\ln a_{k}+\delta, (3) with Φ \Phi the standard normal distribution function, and once the suite is measured the bias is updated by the LMS delta rule [ 57 ] , δ ← ( 1 − η ) ​ δ + η ⁡ ( ln ⁡ s − ln ⁡ a ) \delta\leftarrow(1-\eta)\,\delta+\eta\,(\ln s-\ln a) .

sections.heading: Size-annealing UCB.
sections.text: Niche selection is a bandit whose arms are the niches. The reward of a call is the increment Δ \Delta it adds to the multi-objective QD score [ 45 ] , MOQD ⁡ ( 𝒜 ) = ∑ j HV ⁡ ( 𝒜 j ) \mathrm{MOQD}(\mathcal{A})=\sum_{j}\mathrm{HV}(\mathcal{A}_{j}) , the total area the niche fronts dominate, credited to the niche the suite actually lands in, whether it improves a niche or populates an empty one. The acquisition is UCB ⁡ ( k ) = ∑ j p j ​ ( k ) ​ ( Q ^ j − λ ​ z j ) ⏟ expected exploitation + c e n k + 1 ⏟ exploration , λ = max ⁡ ( 0 , hv best − H ) , \mathrm{UCB}(k)=\underbrace{\sum_{j}p_{j}(k)\big(\widehat{Q}_{j}-\lambda z_{j}\big)}_{\text{expected exploitation}}+\underbrace{\frac{c_{e}}{\sqrt{n_{k}+1}}}_{\text{exploration}},\qquad\lambda=\max\big(0,\ \mathrm{hv}^{\mathrm{best}}-H\big), (4) where Q ^ j ← ( 1 − α ) ​ Q ^ j + α ​ Δ \widehat{Q}_{j}\leftarrow(1-\alpha)\widehat{Q}_{j}+\alpha\Delta is the discounted reward of landing in niche j j , initialized for an unseen niche to the mean over observed ones; z j = ( j − 1 ) / ( K − 1 ) z_{j}=(j-1)/(K-1) is the normalized niche index; n k n_{k} counts the calls aimed at niche k k wherever they landed; and c e c_{e} is an exploration coefficient [ 5 ] . Two details are load-bearing. The kernel weights the exploitation term, because p j ​ ( k ) p_{j}(k) is an actuator outcome distribution rather than a policy prior [ 5 , 27 ] ; and the size penalty sits inside the expectation, so what is penalized is the size a suite lands at, not the size aimed for. The size penalty λ \lambda stays at zero until the best hypervolume found so far reaches a threshold H H , and grows with it afterwards. The search therefore secures quality first and only then favors smaller suites, following the quality-then-size order of Definition 1 .

sections.heading: 5.1 Setup
sections.text: We use the 129 129 distinct Python modules of TestGenEval [ 24 ] , each with a containerized harness. Mutants are produced per module by cosmic-ray [ 50 ] under a fixed seed and split into a search fold, which scores the search, and a held-out eval fold, which scores what is delivered. Every method runs under an identical budget of N = 50 N=50 calls per module, on GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 4.8 and Gemini 3.1 Pro. The baselines are (i) Pynguin [ 35 ] , the reference search-based tool for Python, matched in wall clock ( 6000 6000 s) since it makes no model call; (ii) inference-time scaling: iterative refinement [ 49 ] , best-of- N N [ 32 , 8 ] , beam search of width 5 5 , and the context optimizers MIPROv2 and ACE [ 44 , 68 ] ; GEPA [ 1 ] , whose single global Pareto pool over ( c , m , − s ) (c,m,-s) makes it the three-objective alternative to our formulation; and OpenEvolve [ 43 ] , an open implementation of AlphaEvolve [ 41 ] that evolves suites in a MAP-Elites archive under the same feedback; (iii) the coding agents Claude Code and Cursor [ 3 , 4 ] , told to maximize quality and minimize size, with harness feedback as tool output; and (iv) ablations: w/o kernel asks for the niche center as written and credits each arm where its calls land; w/o UCB sweeps the grid uniformly while keeping the aim; w/o nearest parents samples parents at random from the fronts; w/o λ \lambda sets λ = 0 \lambda=0 . sections.heading: 5.2 Test-suite quality
sections.text: Table 1 reports the delivered suite. tesearch attains the highest hypervolume on every backbone, 7.0 7.0 – 8.5 8.5 points above the strongest baseline, in the smallest suites any LLM-based method delivers. Pynguin delivers fewer tests, but at hv = 0.090 \mathrm{hv}=0.090 : size is a coordinate here, not the objective. The two population-based baselines isolate the formulation. OpenEvolve also keeps an archive and is the strongest baseline on GPT-5.4, but its archive is not indexed by size, so it holds nothing small to hand back and delivers 51.5 51.5 tests. GEPA puts − s -s in the objective, admitting near-empty suites as non-dominated and leaving a front wide in size but shallow in quality. The ablations separate on the axis each mechanism moves: removing λ \lambda costs little quality ( − 0.02 -0.02 to − 0.06 -0.06 hv) but grows suites 1.5 1.5 – 2.9 × 2.9\times ; removing the kernel inflates size hardest where the actuator overshoots most ( + 11.7 +11.7 and + 27.0 +27.0 tests on Claude Opus 4.8 and Gemini 3.1 Pro), since credit piles up in the larger niches that off-target calls reach; removing UCB or the nearest parents costs quality and size on all three backbones. The actuator and the anneal. Over 6063 6063 tesearch generations on GPT-5.4, the count bias δ \delta ranges from − 0.037 -0.037 to + 0.107 +0.107 across modules and changes sign, so no fixed correction serves all; online, the log-size residuals have mean 0.013 0.013 and standard deviation 0.100 0.100 , as the kernel assumes. Allocation is selective without collapsing: grouped into eight normalized size bands, no band falls below a 0.067 0.067 share of calls in any window. Against constant and no size pressure, only the quality-gated ramp finishes both highest in quality and smallest in size.

sections.heading: 5.3 Improvement signal for a self-evolving agent
sections.text: Setup. We study the keep-or-discard decision on mini-swe-agent [ 51 ] , an open variant of SWE-agent [ 61 ] whose harness is a few hundred lines of Python. For each of eight harness modules, GPT-5.4 receives a revision intent drawn from common self-improvement goals (latency, tokens, robustness, structure), either behavior-preserving or behavior-changing, and implements it as a revised module, 64 64 per module; each behavior-changing intent is the failure mode of a preserving one with the same goal and shape of edit, such as caching a function that reads changing state ( Appendix E ). Two annotators verify each revision ( κ = 0.74 \kappa=0.74 ), leaving the 470 470 of Table 2 , labeled divergent if the intent changes behavior and equivalent otherwise. A gate rejects a revision when its suite fails where it passed on the unmodified module; the tesearch suite is generated once from that module and compared with its repository tests. sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: Self-evolving agents now rewrite their own harness fluently; what they cannot yet tell is whether a self-referential edit is correct and leaves existing behavior intact. This paper targets that gap with a quality–diversity evolutionary search that treats suite size as a behavior descriptor, so quality is pursued at every size and a small, strong suite is reachable, and learns a transition kernel during the search that denoises the LLM as an actuator on that descriptor. Across 129 129 modules and three backbones the resulting suites are the strongest of any method compared and the smallest of any LLM-based one, and as the gate of a self-evolving agent they reject 59.9 % 59.9\% of behavior-changing rewrites against 25.3 % 25.3\% for the repository’s tests, at 3.5 3.5 s per decision and no model call. tesearch is thus an effective improvement signal for self-evolving agents: strong enough to catch what a rewrite silently broke, cheap enough to run on every rewrite.

sections.heading: Appendix A The size-niched grid
sections.text: Suite size is the archive’s only descriptor, and the noise on it is multiplicative: asking for twice as many tests does not add a fixed error, it scales the error, which is why Section 4 models landing as log-normal. The grid is therefore a partition of ln ⁡ s \ln s built once, immediately after the seed phase. The grid is centered on an anchor s ¯ \bar{s} , the size the backbone writes at when no size is named, estimated as the geometric mean of the seed suites’ sizes. Writing T 1 , … , T n T_{1},\dots,T_{n} for the n n seed suites that measured, s ¯ = exp ⁡ ( 1 n ​ ∑ i = 1 n ln ⁡ s ⁡ ( T i ) ) . \bar{s}\;=\;\exp\!\Big(\tfrac{1}{n}\sum\nolimits_{i=1}^{n}\ln s(T_{i})\Big). (5) The mean is taken on the log scale because the noise is multiplicative, and the seeds are unhinted precisely so that the anchor measures the model rather than our own prompt. Niches are geometric, with equal width on the log scale. This is the spacing used whenever values within a constant factor of each other are interchangeable, as in MetaGrad’s exponentially spaced grid of learning rates [ 53 ] , and whenever error is relative rather than absolute, as in DDSketch, whose bucket ratio is set by the relative accuracy it guarantees [ 38 ] . Under multiplicative noise, both hold for suite sizes. Consecutive niches differ by the ratio ρ = e 2 ​ σ = 1.22 \rho=e^{2\sigma}=1.22 , where σ = 0.10 \sigma=0.10 is the landing spread of the transition kernel ( Section 4 ), so each niche spans ± σ \pm\sigma around its center on the log scale. This width is intended: since Section 4 models landing noise as log-normal, an aimed draw lands in the niche it was aimed at with probability 68 % 68\% under the model. The grid is built per module over the range [ s min , s ¯ ​ ρ γ ] [s_{\min},\,\bar{s}\rho^{\gamma}] , and both ends follow conventions of software testing [ 52 , 40 ] . The lower end is set by the module: s min s_{\min} is the number of public functions and methods of the module under test, counted statically from its AST. A suite with fewer tests than that must check several of them in one test method, which is the Eager Test smell: such a test is hard to read, hard to use as documentation of the behavior it checks, and makes tests more dependent on each other, and the prescribed remedy is to split it until each test method exercises a single method of the unit [ 52 ] . The floor also guards against reward hacking, in which the LLM packs all its checks into a single test function to game the size reward. The upper end is relative to the anchor, γ \gamma niches above it, and so scales with the size of the module. In software testing, the effectiveness of a suite grows with its size [ 23 ] , but only logarithmically [ 40 ] . Beyond a minimal suite, one from which no test can be removed without lowering its mutation score, further tests add nothing but code smells such as Lazy Test and Test Code Duplication [ 52 ] . To keep suite size from growing without bound, and to avoid spending calls on unreasonably large suites, we set γ = 4 \gamma=4 . The boundaries that fall inside the range, sorted and with duplicates dropped, are b 1 < ⋯ < b K − 1 b_{1}<\dots<b_{K-1} . A suite outside the range is filed rather than dropped, into one of two open overflow niches, [ 0 , b 1 ) [0,b_{1}) and [ b K − 1 , ∞ ) [b_{K-1},\infty) ; the bandit never aims at them, and a call that lands in one is still charged to the arm it aimed at.

sections.heading: Appendix C Parent selection and context assembly
sections.text: Given the selected niche k ∗ k^{\ast} , tesearch selects two parents from all Pareto-front suites in the archive, rather than only from the target niche. Specifically, one parent is taken from each side of the target size: on each side, suites are ranked by their log-size distance to the target, | ln ⁡ s ⁡ ( T ) − ln ⁡ τ k ∗ | , \left|\ln s(T)-\ln\tau_{k^{\ast}}\right|, with hypervolume breaking ties, and the nearest suite is selected. Using the global archive allows generation even when the target niche is empty, while size proximity provides examples at a scale close to the requested suite. The generation context consists of the module under test, execution feedback, the two selected parents, and the requested size. Execution feedback highlights uncovered lines and surviving mutants. The parents are ordered from weaker to stronger, placing the stronger example closest to the generation request. Finally, the LLM is instructed to generate a suite of the requested size by compressing or extending the last parent, according to whether the target lies below or above it. Appendix D provides the full prompt.

sections.heading: Parent selection.
sections.text: Parents are selected by size proximity from the two sides of the target: the Pareto-front suite nearest τ k ∗ \tau_{k^{\ast}} in log size among those smaller than the target, and the nearest among those larger. Because the grid is geometric, the niche index is log size up to a constant, so each side is a one-dimensional nearest-neighbor lookup. The two parents therefore always differ in size, and their relation in Table 3 follows from their hypervolumes: if the smaller parent has no lower hypervolume, it Pareto-dominates the larger one; otherwise the larger one lexicographically dominates it. When one side has no suite, the parents come from the other side alone; in that edge case the call must compress or expand the suite toward the target while raising its hypervolume. The pool is global rather than niche-local for a structural reason: the acquisition frequently selects a niche no suite has reached yet, and a draw restricted to that niche’s own front would leave exactly those targets unbreedable. The w/o nearest-parents ablation replaces the ranking with a uniform draw over the same pool and changes nothing else — the candidates are still front members, so nothing dominated is ever shown, and the ordering rule below still applies.

sections.heading: Ordering and annotation.
sections.text: The two parents and the target are arranged ascending under the order of Definition 1 — by hypervolume first, and by smaller size only when hypervolumes are equal — with the target always last, immediately before the continuation, where recency weighs the nearest example most [ 70 , 33 , 60 ] . With one parent on each side of the target size, the arrangement takes one of two mirror forms ( Table 4 ). If the larger parent L L has the higher hypervolume, the order is S , L , T S,L,T : L L lexicographically dominates S S , and the target T T must Pareto-dominate L L , compressing it to the target size at no lower hypervolume. Otherwise the order is L , S , T L,S,T : S S Pareto-dominates L L , and T T must lexicographically dominate S S , expanding it to the target size at strictly higher hypervolume. The asymmetry is deliberate: a smaller suite at equal hypervolume is already an improvement under Definition 1 , and the only one left once hypervolume saturates, whereas a larger suite is worth its extra tests only if it raises hypervolume. The second parent carries a one-line note comparing it with the first, in one of the two forms of Table 3 ; the note states the measured change in both hypervolume and size, so it is always a measured claim rather than an inferred narrative. sections.heading: Appendix D Prompt construction
sections.text: With the two parents chosen and ordered ( Appendix C ), three further decisions turn them into a prompt: which of the two breeding framings the call is given, what execution signal is written into the module source, and how much of each piece is shown.

sections.heading: Feedback signal.
sections.text: The module source shown in a breeding prompt is annotated with what the strongest parent still misses, written at the end of the exact line it describes rather than as a separate list of line numbers: # <-- NOT COVERED YET on a line none of its passing tests execute, and # <-- SURVIVING MUTANT: <op> on a line where that mutation survives its assertions. Failing tests inside an example suite are marked the same way, at the end of the (possibly multi-line) def header, as # <-- FAILING: <exception> . Adjacency is the point: models align a mark sitting next to the code far more reliably than a position given in a distant block of text. Coverage only ever flags executable statement lines, so a trailing comment is syntactically safe wherever a mark can land.

You will be shown EXISTING versions of this suite , ordered from weakest to strongest by hypervolume ( coverage x mutation - kill ), the smaller one ranking stronger when hypervolumes are equal ; the LAST one is the strongest shown . Each is labeled with its own size / coverage / mutation - kill numbers , and the second carries a short , factual note comparing it to the version immediately before it . Some tests in the versions you are shown FAIL against the module as given ; each is marked ‘# <-- FAILING : < exception >‘ at the end of its ‘ def ‘ line , and the numbers in that version ’ s header were measured on its PASSING tests only . Rewrite that version DOWN to the target size with a hypervolume at least as high as its own , and higher if you can : merge related assertions into fewer , denser tests ; share setup ; fold parametrizable cases together with pytest . mark . parametrize ; drop only what is truly redundant . Do not pad with redundant tests - every added test should close an annotated gap . Failing tests carry real testing intent - REPAIR them by reading the module source and fixing the expected value , rather than deleting them , unless the same behaviour is already checked elsewhere . sections.heading: Self-evolving agents in verticals.
sections.text: A general-purpose agent becomes useful in a vertical domain through knowledge its weights do not hold, and with frozen weights ( Section 2 ) it evolves by how that knowledge is streamed in, managed and retrieved. Streaming turns raw domain input, arriving continuously, into a structured form an agent can consume: knowledge graphs constructed from unstructured threat reports [ 10 ] , hybrid system logs parsed by a user-adaptive parser [ 59 ] , and natural language translated into first-order logic that symbolic reasoners can consume [ 46 ] . Management organizes and revises what has been accumulated: cyber threat intelligence (CTI) corpora organized into agent-native scaffolds that agents consume directly [ 13 ] , documentation optimized as repository-specific playbooks for coding agents [ 12 ] , and behavioral specifications of program entities refined recursively from the failures of the code generated from them [ 11 ] , where a local improvement must be kept from causing a regression elsewhere. Retrieval decides what of it reaches the agent at decision time, as benchmarked for retrieval-augmented LLMs over heterogeneous CTI sources [ 14 ] . Across the three stages, what lets a vertical agent evolve rather than drift is a signal, grounded in its domain, that decides which revisions of its knowledge to keep: knowledge graphs, corpora and parsers are typically judged once, by extraction or answer accuracy, and specifications and documentation by tests taken as given. This paper turns to that signal itself. In software, where it is executable, we search for the test suite that serves as it, strong enough to catch a revision that silently changes behavior and small enough to run on every revision, whether what is revised is documentation, a specification or, as in Section 5.3 , the agent’s own harness.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.15964v1 [cs.AI] 11 Oct 2026 \workshoptitle Self-Evolving Diversity-Driven Search for Robust AI Systems Small but Mighty: Test Suites as Improvement Signals for Self-Evolving Agents Yutong Cheng † † thanks: Work done during the internship at NEC Laboratories America. Affiliation: Virginia Tech Email: yutongcheng@vt.edu Wei Cheng Affiliation: NEC Laboratories America Email: zhoud@vt.edu Wenchao Yu Affiliation: NEC Laboratories America Email: weicheng@nec-labs.com Dawei Zhou Affiliation: Virginia Tech Email: wyu@nec-labs.com Haifeng Chen Affiliation: NEC Laboratories America Email: haifeng@nec-labs.com Abstract A self-evolving agent rewrites its own harness and must decide which rewrites to keep, so its improvement signal is the check a rewrite has to pass. Verifying a rewrite by agent rollout is expensive and subjective, while executable checks such as the repository’s own tests are too sparse to catch behavior-changing rewrites, rejecting only a quarter of them. We instead take test feedback as the executable signal, and search for test suites that are both small and strong with a quality–diversity evolutionary algorithm, so that the signal is dense and informative. tesearch treats suite size as a behavior descriptor, so that quality is pursued at every size and a small, strong suite is reachable, and learns a transition kernel during the search that denoises the LLM as an actuator on that descriptor. Across 129 129 real-world modules and three backbones, tesearch delivers the highest-quality suites of any method compared, LLM-driven evolutionary search included, and the smallest of any LLM-based one. Used as the improvement signal of a self-evolving agent, it rejects 59.9 % 59.9\% of behavior-changing rewrites against 25.3 % 25.3\% for the repository’s tests, at a 4.0 % 4.0\% false-alarm rate and 3.5 3.5 s per decision. The code and data are available at https://github.com/ccsnow127/TeSearch . 1 Introduction Self-evolving agents get stronger by editing the code that runs them: the harness that prompts the model, parses its actions, executes them and records the trajectory [ 34 , 55 , 67 ] . The check a rewrite must pass to be kept is the agent’s improvement signal . Accept a rewrite that silently changes behavior and every later episode and rewrite inherits it; reject rewrites that preserve behavior and the evolution stalls. In software engineering the executable form of this check is the test suite, a regression specification [ 62 ] that captures the accepted behavior of the code so that later modification can preserve it. The signals available today are weak. Accepting on rollout outcome spends an agent episode per candidate on a noisy end-to-end score. The repository’s own tests are free, but they were written before the agent existed and anticipate none of its edits: we find them rejecting only 25.3 % 25.3\% of the rewrites that change behavior ( Section 5.3 ). A generated suite can do better, but only if it is effective , so that a behavioral change breaks at least one test, and efficient , since it runs on every proposed rewrite and its failures are read by a model with a finite context. Existing generators, search-based or LLM-based, optimize effectiveness and leave size to whatever emerges [ 18 , 35 , 2 , 24 ] . We formulate size-optimized unit test generation and, rather than scalarizing quality against size, let size define where a suite competes and quality whether it wins : size is a behavior descriptor of a quality–diversity (QD) search [ 39 , 45 ] , so the small end stays alive instead of being eliminated by the large one. Two challenges follow. LLM calls are expensive, so a finite budget must be allocated across niches whose value is unknown. And unlike classical QD, the descriptor cannot be set directly: the search can only ask the LLM for a count, which LLMs follow imprecisely [ 71 ] , so the niche a call targets and the niche it lands in differ. tesearch answers both: an online landing kernel models the LLM as a noisy actuator on the descriptor, correcting its bias and predicting where each call lands, and a size-annealing UCB allocates calls across niches from those predictions, turning toward smaller suites only once quality is secured. Its suites are the strongest and, among LLM-based methods, the smallest on 129 129 real-world modules, and as the improvement signal of a self-evolving agent they more than double the detection of behavior-changing rewrites at a cost the loop can afford on every one. 2 Related work Self-evolving agents and improvement signals. Self-improving LLM systems differ first in where an improvement is written. Weight-space methods fine-tune the model on its own data or rewards [ 56 , 74 , 73 ] , a gain that cannot be read, diffed or reverted. Context-space methods write into the harness instead, through verbal self-refinement [ 37 , 49 ] , prompt search and textual gradients [ 60 , 64 , 44 , 1 ] , experience memory [ 68 ] , skill synthesis [ 54 ] or search over the whole scaffold [ 22 ] ; at the frontier the agent rewrites its own code, including the procedure that performs the update [ 17 , 65 , 67 , 34 ] . What decides whether an improvement is kept ranges from the model’s own judgment [ 6 , 63 ] to external verifiers such as tests [ 7 , 9 ] , compilers [ 29 , 20 ] and environments [ 36 ] . Tests are the signal coding agents such as Cursor, Codex and Claude Code [ 4 , 42 , 3 ] lean on across whole repositories [ 26 , 61 , 66 ] , yet they are taken as given: the repository’s own or written ad hoc. We optimize the test signal itself, for the strength and cost a loop running it on every rewrite needs. See Appendix F for additional related work. Evolutionary and quality–diversity search. LLMs used as variation operators under executable fitness make evolutionary search a strong inference-time optimizer [ 47 , 41 , 28 ] , but a global objective concentrates the population around one mode [ 19 , 16 ] . QD optimization instead partitions the search space by behavior descriptors and optimizes quality within each region [ 30 , 15 ] : MAP-Elites keeps an elite per cell [ 39 ] , and MOME a Pareto front per cell whose hypervolumes it sums [ 45 ] . Search-based test generation evolves program inputs against coverage goals [ 18 , 35 ] and test-suite reduction shrinks a written suite post hoc [ 21 , 48 ] ; neither controls size during generation. In classical QD the descriptor is read off what an individual turns out to be; here it must be requested from an LLM before it can be observed, and tesearch models that actuation error explicitly. 3 Size-optimized test generation Given a Python module M M , a suite T T is a finite set of test functions for M M , with size s ⁡ ( T ) s(T) . Two objectives are measured on it: coverage c ⁡ ( T ) ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] c(T)\in[0,1] , the fraction of executable lines of M M executed, and mutation score m ⁡ ( T ) ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] m(T)\in[0,1] , the fraction of a fixed sample of mutants of M M killed [ 25 ] . With the origin as reference, a suite has hypervolume hv ⁡ ( T ) = c ⁡ ( T ) ​ m ​ ( T ) \mathrm{hv}(T)=c(T)\,m(T) [ 72 ] , high only when both objectives are. Definition 1 (Size-optimized unit test generation) . Given a module M M and executable quality metrics ( c , m ) (c,m) , produce a collection 𝒯 \mathcal{T} of suites and deliver the smallest suite of maximal hypervolume: T ⋆ = arg ​ min T ∈ 𝒯 max ⁡ s ​ ( T ) , 𝒯 max = arg ​ max T ∈ 𝒯 ⁡ hv ​ ( T ) . T^{\star}\;=\;\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{T\in\mathcal{T}^{\max}}s(T),\qquad\mathcal{T}^{\max}\;=\;\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{T\in\mathcal{T}}\mathrm{hv}(T). Quality–diversity formulation. Definition 1 is the terminal objective; QD is the search surrogate. Larger suites are naturally advantaged in a global competition on ( c , m ) (c,m) [ 40 , 23 ] , so size becomes the behavior descriptor and quality is optimized independently within size niches, each keeping a Pareto front over ( c , m ) (c,m) rather than a single elite [ 45 ] : 𝒜 j = nd ( c , m ) { T ∈ 𝒯 : b j − 1 ≤ s ( T ) < b j } , j = 1 , … , K , \mathcal{A}_{j}=\operatorname*{nd}_{(c,m)}\big\{\,T\in\mathcal{T}:b_{j-1}\leq s(T)<b_{j}\big\},\qquad j=1,\dots,K, (1) where nd \operatorname{nd} takes the non-dominated subset and b 0 < ⋯ < b K b_{0}<\dots<b_{K} are the niche boundaries, the outermost two left open ( b 0 = 0 b_{0}=0 , b K = ∞ b_{K}=\infty ). The niches are geometric, since the variation in generated size grows with the size requested ( Appendix A ). Search loop and challenges. Each iteration ( Figure 1 ) selects a target niche; takes as parents the Pareto-front suite nearest the target in log size on each side of it, ordered weaker to stronger since an LLM weighs its most recent context most; prompts the LLM with the parents, the module annotated with its uncovered lines and surviving mutants, and the target size ( Appendices C and D ); then scores the suite and files it where it actually lands ( Algorithm 1 ). The two challenges are allocation of the call budget and actuation . 4 tesearch Figure 1: Overview of tesearch . The archive (bottom) keeps a Pareto front on (coverage, mutation score) per size niche. (1) Size-UCB picks a target niche through the transition kernel; (2) the nearest front suite on each side of the target size becomes a parent; (3) parents, module, execution feedback and target size form the context; (4) the LLM writes a suite, possibly off the requested size; (5) the suite is filed where it lands, and the size error updates the kernel. The landing kernel. Requesting a suite of size a a may produce one of size s ≠ a s\neq a , so a call aimed at one niche may land in another and credit assigned to the target goes to the wrong arm. LLMs follow count instructions with multiplicative noise [ 69 , 31 , 58 ] , so we model landing in log space, ln ⁡ s ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( ln ⁡ a + δ , σ 2 ) , \ln s\;\sim\;\mathcal{N}\big(\ln a+\delta,\ \sigma^{2}\big), (2) with δ \delta the systematic count bias and σ \sigma the residual spread. The bias varies across modules and backbones and enters the request directly, so it is estimated online and compensated before generation: for a target niche k k with center τ k = b k − 1 ​ b k \tau_{k}=\sqrt{b_{k-1}b_{k}} , inverting Equation 2 gives the request ln ⁡ a k = ln ⁡ τ k − δ \ln a_{k}=\ln\tau_{k}-\delta , rounded to an integer. The spread only spreads credit over neighboring niches; it is stable and fixed at its holdout median. The landing distribution of a call aimed at niche k k is p j ​ ( k ) = Φ ⁡ ( ln ⁡ b j − μ k σ ) − Φ ⁡ ( ln ⁡ b j − 1 − μ k σ ) , μ k = ln ⁡ a k + δ , p_{j}(k)=\Phi\!\Big(\tfrac{\ln b_{j}-\mu_{k}}{\sigma}\Big)-\Phi\!\Big(\tfrac{\ln b_{j-1}-\mu_{k}}{\sigma}\Big),\qquad\mu_{k}=\ln a_{k}+\delta, (3) with Φ \Phi the standard normal distribution function, and once the suite is measured the bias is updated by the LMS delta rule [ 57 ] , δ ← ( 1 − η ) ​ δ + η ⁡ ( ln ⁡ s − ln ⁡ a ) \delta\leftarrow(1-\eta)\,\delta+\eta\,(\ln s-\ln a) . Size-annealing UCB. Niche selection is a bandit whose arms are the niches. The reward of a call is the increment Δ \Delta it adds to the multi-objective QD score [ 45 ] , MOQD ⁡ ( 𝒜 ) = ∑ j HV ⁡ ( 𝒜 j ) \mathrm{MOQD}(\mathcal{A})=\sum_{j}\mathrm{HV}(\mathcal{A}_{j}) , the total area the niche fronts dominate, credited to the niche the suite actually lands in, whether it improves a niche or populates an empty one. The acquisition is UCB ⁡ ( k ) = ∑ j p j ​ ( k ) ​ ( Q ^ j − λ ​ z j ) ⏟ expected exploitation + c e n k + 1 ⏟ exploration , λ = max ⁡ ( 0 , hv best − H ) , \mathrm{UCB}(k)=\underbrace{\sum_{j}p_{j}(k)\big(\widehat{Q}_{j}-\lambda z_{j}\big)}_{\text{expected exploitation}}+\underbrace{\frac{c_{e}}{\sqrt{n_{k}+1}}}_{\text{exploration}},\qquad\lambda=\max\big(0,\ \mathrm{hv}^{\mathrm{best}}-H\big), (4) where Q ^ j ← ( 1 − α ) ​ Q ^ j + α ​ Δ \widehat{Q}_{j}\leftarrow(1-\alpha)\widehat{Q}_{j}+\alpha\Delta is the discounted reward of landing in niche j j , initialized for an unseen niche to the mean over observed ones; z j = ( j − 1 ) / ( K − 1 ) z_{j}=(j-1)/(K-1) is the normalized niche index; n k n_{k} counts the calls aimed at niche k k wherever they landed; and c e c_{e} is an exploration coefficient [ 5 ] . Two details are load-bearing. The kernel weights the exploitation term, because p j ​ ( k ) p_{j}(k) is an actuator outcome distribution rather than a policy prior [ 5 , 27 ] ; and the size penalty sits inside the expectation, so what is penalized is the size a suite lands at, not the size aimed for. The size penalty λ \lambda stays at zero until the best hypervolume found so far reaches a threshold H H , and grows with it afterwards. The search therefore secures quality first and only then favors smaller suites, following the quality-then-size order of Definition 1 . 5 Experiments 5.1 Setup We use the 129 129 distinct Python modules of TestGenEval [ 24 ] , each with a containerized harness. Mutants are produced per module by cosmic-ray [ 50 ] under a fixed seed and split into a search fold, which scores the search, and a held-out eval fold, which scores what is delivered. Every method runs under an identical budget of N = 50 N=50 calls per module, on GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 4.8 and Gemini 3.1 Pro. The baselines are (i) Pynguin [ 35 ] , the reference search-based tool for Python, matched in wall clock ( 6000 6000 s) since it makes no model call; (ii) inference-time scaling: iterative refinement [ 49 ] , best-of- N N [ 32 , 8 ] , beam search of width 5 5 , and the context optimizers MIPROv2 and ACE [ 44 , 68 ] ; GEPA [ 1 ] , whose single global Pareto pool over ( c , m , − s ) (c,m,-s) makes it the three-objective alternative to our formulation; and OpenEvolve [ 43 ] , an open implementation of AlphaEvolve [ 41 ] that evolves suites in a MAP-Elites archive under the same feedback; (iii) the coding agents Claude Code and Cursor [ 3 , 4 ] , told to maximize quality and minimize size, with harness feedback as tool output; and (iv) ablations: w/o kernel asks for the niche center as written and credits each arm where its calls land; w/o UCB sweeps the grid uniformly while keeping the aim; w/o nearest parents samples parents at random from the fronts; w/o λ \lambda sets λ = 0 \lambda=0 . Pynguin delivers fewer tests, but at hv = 0.090 \mathrm{hv}=0.090 : size is a coordinate here, not the objective. The two population-based baselines isolate the formulation. OpenEvolve also keeps an archive and is the strongest baseline on GPT-5.4, but its archive is not indexed by size, so it holds nothing small to hand back and delivers 51.5 51.5 tests. GEPA puts − s -s in the objective, admitting near-empty suites as non-dominated and leaving a front wide in size but shallow in quality. The ablations separate on the axis each mechanism moves: removing λ \lambda costs little quality ( − 0.02 -0.02 to − 0.06 -0.06 hv) but grows suites 1.5 1.5 – 2.9 × 2.9\times ; removing the kernel inflates size hardest where the actuator overshoots most ( + 11.7 +11.7 and + 27.0 +27.0 tests on Claude Opus 4.8 and Gemini 3.1 Pro), since credit piles up in the larger niches that off-target calls reach; removing UCB or the nearest parents costs quality and size on all three backbones. The actuator and the anneal. Over 6063 6063 tesearch generations on GPT-5.4, the count bias δ \delta ranges from − 0.037 -0.037 to + 0.107 +0.107 across modules and changes sign, so no fixed correction serves all; online, the log-size residuals have mean 0.013 0.013 and standard deviation 0.100 0.100 , as the kernel assumes. Allocation is selective without collapsing: grouped into eight normalized size bands, no band falls below a 0.067 0.067 share of calls in any window. Against constant and no size pressure, only the quality-gated ramp finishes both highest in quality and smallest in size. 5.3 Improvement signal for a self-evolving agent Setup. We study the keep-or-discard decision on mini-swe-agent [ 51 ] , an open variant of SWE-agent [ 61 ] whose harness is a few hundred lines of Python. For each of eight harness modules, GPT-5.4 receives a revision intent drawn from common self-improvement goals (latency, tokens, robustness, structure), either behavior-preserving or behavior-changing, and implements it as a revised module, 64 64 per module; each behavior-changing intent is the failure mode of a preserving one with the same goal and shape of edit, such as caching a function that reads changing state ( Appendix E ). Two annotators verify each revision ( κ = 0.74 \kappa=0.74 ), leaving the 470 470 of Table 2 , labeled divergent if the intent changes behavior and equivalent otherwise. A gate rejects a revision when its suite fails where it passed on the unmodified module; the tesearch suite is generated once from that module and compared with its repository tests. Repository tests check that a module performs its function; a mutation-optimized suite also pins the details a mutant perturbs, such as a separator, a default or which exception surfaces, so the gap is widest on modules that parse model outputs or render what the model reads. The tighter constraint costs little: tesearch rejects 10 10 of the 253 253 equivalent revisions, a 4.0 % 4.0\% false-alarm rate, where the repository tests reject none. A decision takes 3.5 3.5 s against 5.9 5.9 s and calls no model, where acceptance by rollout spends an agent episode: the agent can afford this signal on every rewrite it proposes. 6 Conclusion Self-evolving agents now rewrite their own harness fluently; what they cannot yet tell is whether a self-referential edit is correct and leaves existing behavior intact. This paper targets that gap with a quality–diversity evolutionary search that treats suite size as a behavior descriptor, so quality is pursued at every size and a small, strong suite is reachable, and learns a transition kernel during the search that denoises the LLM as an actuator on that descriptor. Across 129 129 modules and three backbones the resulting suites are the strongest of any method compared and the smallest of any LLM-based one, and as the gate of a self-evolving agent they reject 59.9 % 59.9\% of behavior-changing rewrites against 25.3 % 25.3\% for the repository’s tests, at 3.5 3.5 s per decision and no model call. tesearch is thus an effective improvement signal for self-evolving agents: strong enough to catch what a rewrite silently broke, cheap enough to run on every rewrite. Specifically, one parent is taken from each side of the target size: on each side, suites are ranked by their log-size distance to the target, | ln ⁡ s ⁡ ( T ) − ln ⁡ τ k ∗ | , \left|\ln s(T)-\ln\tau_{k^{\ast}}\right|, with hypervolume breaking ties, and the nearest suite is selected. Using the global archive allows generation even when the target niche is empty, while size proximity provides examples at a scale close to the requested suite. The generation context consists of the module under test, execution feedback, the two selected parents, and the requested size. Execution feedback highlights uncovered lines and surviving mutants. The parents are ordered from weaker to stronger, placing the stronger example closest to the generation request. Finally, the LLM is instructed to generate a suite of the requested size by compressing or extending the last parent, according to whether the target lies below or above it. Appendix D provides the full prompt. Parent selection. Parents are selected by size proximity from the two sides of the target: the Pareto-front suite nearest τ k ∗ \tau_{k^{\ast}} in log size among those smaller than the target, and the nearest among those larger. Because the grid is geometric, the niche index is log size up to a constant, so each side is a one-dimensional nearest-neighbor lookup. The two parents therefore always differ in size, and their relation in Table 3 follows from their hypervolumes: if the smaller parent has no lower hypervolume, it Pareto-dominates the larger one; otherwise the larger one lexicographically dominates it. When one side has no suite, the parents come from the other side alone; in that edge case the call must compress or expand the suite toward the target while raising its hypervolume. The pool is global rather than niche-local for a structural reason: the acquisition frequently selects a niche no suite has reached yet, and a draw restricted to that niche’s own front would leave exactly those targets unbreedable. The w/o nearest-parents ablation replaces the ranking with a uniform draw over the same pool and changes nothing else — the candidates are still front members, so nothing dominated is ever shown, and the ordering rule below still applies. Feedback signal. The module source shown in a breeding prompt is annotated with what the strongest parent still misses, written at the end of the exact line it describes rather than as a separate list of line numbers: # <-- NOT COVERED YET on a line none of its passing tests execute, and # <-- SURVIVING MUTANT: <op> on a line where that mutation survives its assertions. Failing tests inside an example suite are marked the same way, at the end of the (possibly multi-line) def header, as # <-- FAILING: <exception> . Adjacency is the point: models align a mark sitting next to the code far more reliably than a position given in a distant block of text. Coverage only ever flags executable statement lines, so a trailing comment is syntactically safe wherever a mark can land. Prompts, verbatim. A general-purpose agent becomes useful in a vertical domain through knowledge its weights do not hold, and with frozen weights ( Section 2 ) it evolves by how that knowledge is streamed in, managed and retrieved. Streaming turns raw domain input, arriving continuously, into a structured form an agent can consume: knowledge graphs constructed from unstructured threat reports [ 10 ] , hybrid system logs parsed by a user-adaptive parser [ 59 ] , and natural language translated into first-order logic that symbolic reasoners can consume [ 46 ] . Management organizes and revises what has been accumulated: cyber threat intelligence (CTI) corpora organized into agent-native scaffolds that agents consume directly [ 13 ] , documentation optimized as repository-specific playbooks for coding agents [ 12 ] , and behavioral specifications of program entities refined recursively from the failures of the code generated from them [ 11 ] , where a local improvement must be kept from causing a regression elsewhere. Retrieval decides what of it reaches the agent at decision time, as benchmarked for retrieval-augmented LLMs over heterogeneous CTI sources [ 14 ] . Across the three stages, what lets a vertical agent evolve rather than drift is a signal, grounded in its domain, that decides which revisions of its knowledge to keep: knowledge graphs, corpora and parsers are typically judged once, by extraction or answer accuracy, and specifications and documentation by tests taken as given. This paper turns to that signal itself. In software, where it is executable, we search for the test suite that serves as it, strong enough to catch a revision that silently changes behavior and small enough to run on every revision, whether what is revised is documentation, a specification or, as in Section 5.3 , the agent’s own harness.
